paras: The lynching of Joseph Smith was the hanging of Joe or Joseph Smith, a Black man, by a mob that took him from the Putnam County jail at Winfield, West Virginia, in the early hours of April 7, 1882. Smith had been jailed about a week earlier, accused of assaulting Mrs. Hill, the wife of a Chesapeake and Ohio Railway section hand, near Scott Station. Dispatches dwelt on the mob's method: sixty to seventy-five men seized a river steamer at Raymond City to reach Winfield.

According to a Charleston special to the Richmond Dispatch, Mrs. Hill was on her way to a neighbor's house near Scott station when she was attacked, and Smith, described as "a negro farm-hand who lived near there," was arrested a few hours later. The Staunton Vindicator dated the assault March 31, which agrees with the Wheeling Intelligencer's "last Friday," while other dispatches said ten days or two weeks earlier.

Smith was held in the jail at Winfield, the county seat of Putnam County. The Putnam Democrat, as summarized by the Point Pleasant Weekly Register, reported that he confessed after his arrest and that a first attempt to lynch him was frustrated by "the prompt action of the Sheriff."

On the night of Thursday, April 6, a body of men took possession of the steamer Sallie Freeze at Raymond City, twelve miles below Charleston, forced its crew to take them to Winfield, and took Smith from the jail.

According to the dispatches, which gave the lynchers' version, Smith said "yes" when the mob asked whether he was guilty and was allowed time to pray before he was hanged from a tree. The Intelligencer put the hanging at 1:30 in the morning of April 7. The body was left hanging until a doctor, whom the Vindicator said the mob had "pressed into service," pronounced Smith dead.

The men returned to Raymond City and paid the captain for the use of his boat, and the people of Winfield found the body in the morning. The Dispatch called the mob "quiet and orderly," and a Pittsburgh dispatch in the Washington Evening Critic said the lynchers were railroad men who acted after hearing that Smith had boasted in jail.

Dispatches reported that Mrs. Hill was dying from the shock, and the Intelligencer gave this as the reason for the hanging, while the Evening Critic said instead that she had been "partially insane" since the assault. No report of an inquest, of arrests of mob members or of grand jury action appears in the coverage, including the local weeklies of the following week.

The first report appeared on April 7 in the Evening Critic, whose Pittsburgh dispatch was headed "A Brute Lynched In Ohio" and placed Winfield in a "Raymond County, Ohio." On April 8 an Associated Press dispatch from Charleston ran in the Wheeling Intelligencer, the Wheeling Register, the Savannah Morning News and the New-York Tribune, and the fuller Charleston special to the Richmond Dispatch was reprinted the same day in the Alexandria Gazette.

West Virginia headlines endorsed the hanging: the Wheeling Register titled the wire "Deserved His Fate," and the Intelligencer ran its own special as "Smith's Swing" with the line "A Richly Merited Fate." That special was reprinted in the South Branch Intelligencer, the New Dominion and the West Virginia Freeman, which printed the mob as "600 men." Short news-summary versions ran from Sacramento to Wilmington, two of them naming the victim "South," and a later weekly digest gave the boat as the "Sally Breeze" and Raymond City as being in "S. C."

Nearly every item stated the accusation as fact, calling Smith "the culprit" or saying he "had committed an outrage." One weekly digest departed from this, writing that the mob hanged him "after extorting a confession from the prisoner."

Accounts differ on where Smith was hanged: the Dispatch said a tree about 300 yards out of town, the Intelligencer a tree "near the town," and the Putnam Democrat, through the Weekly Register, a tree in the Court House yard.

The mob numbered sixty in the Associated Press and Intelligencer reports and about seventy-five in the Dispatch and the Putnam Democrat. Most reports called the offense an outrage or rape, while the Putnam Democrat and the Huntington Advertiser called it an attempted rape.

reader.title: Lynching of Joseph Smith
bases: A mob of sixty to seventy-five men took Smith from the Winfield jail and hanged him to a tree (A2, A10, A15).

A mob of sixty or more broke Smith out of the county jail and hanged him, without lawful authority, on an accusation of assaulting a white woman, which the Intelligencer gave as the reason for the hanging (A2, A10, A13, A15).

The AP wire, a separate Charleston special to the Richmond Dispatch, the Intelligencer's special and the Putnam Democrat (via the Weekly Register) independently agree on the jail seizure and hanging (A7, A2, A10, A15).

framing.detail: The Intelligencer headed its special 'Smith's Swing ... A Richly Merited Fate' and said the woman's condition was the reason for the hanging.
The Evening Critic headed the item 'A Brute Lynched In Ohio.'
Savannah, New York and Sacramento papers ran the wire or a one-line brief without comment.
A weekly digest treated the outrage as fact but wrote that the mob got its confession by 'extorting' it.
